title.narrative: Promoting peace and stability in Iraq by facilitating sustainable returns

description.narrative: After more than two years since the official declaration of the end of war against ISIL by the Government of Iraq in late 2017, approximately 1.4 million people are still internally displaced. Many of the internally displaced persons who are originally from Sinjar are caught in protracted displacement, in which they are displaced for almost six years. Studies show that destruction and/or damage to former residences, lack of basic services due to severe damage to public facilities, and the lack of housing, land and property rights documentation are among common obstacles to return. According to the housing damage assessment jointly conducted by UN-Habitat and Shelter Cluster Iraq, there are 4,570 severely damaged or destroyed houses in Sinjar, and as of end of June 2020, approximately 3,000 houses in Sinjar are left without support. While Yazidis are gradually, and fearfully, returning to the retaken areas of Sinjar north of the mountain, the majority of the region’s Yazidis still live under difficult and impoverished conditions in IDP camps scattered throughout the Dohuk region of northern Iraq. Among the displaced people in Iraq, the Yazidis constitute the second largest group after Arab Sunni Muslims. In Sinjar, the original inhabitants were mostly Yazidis with a small number of Arab Sunnis, Arab Shia, Kurds and Christian population. With the recent outbreak of COVID-19, surveys show that more internally displaced persons in Iraq are willing to return to their areas of origin, trying to avoid congested living conditions with inadequate water and sanitation facilities in many of the camps. On the other hand, many conflict-affected areas including Sinjar still have not managed to rehabilitate water, sanitation, hygiene and health facilities that were damaged during the conflict. In order to prevent the ‘secondary displacement’ of those who returned, it is critical to ensure that adequate housing, water, sanitation and hygiene facilities are available in the areas of origin. Based on the findings of an initial rapid assessment, UN-Habitat will take into consideration the needs of all the population in Sinjar to select the most vulnerable community. Through implemented activities, UN-Habitat will target different vulnerable groups of the recent returnees including minorities in Sinjar district. In addition, based on the assessment the project will consider the provision of the support on HLP rights, rehabilitation of the houses based on physical level of damage, rehabilitation of the water, hygiene and sanitation facilities, based on the socio-economic vulnerability of beneficiaries such as Yazidis, including Arabs and Kurds, to promote voluntary and sustainable return and peace building in Sinjar. Aiming at providing land tenure security, adequate housing for returnees, and access to adequate water, sanitation and hygiene facilities, ensure livelihood opportunities and accessibility of various services, including economic activities and legal that will enable business ownership for minorities including women in a conflict-affected district of Sinjar in Iraq, this project addresses the core of the HDP nexus. It carries humanitarian, development and peace components and brings together stakeholders of each of these three fields. First, the humanitarian component is reflected in the urgent assistance of the most vulnerable for the access to housing and water. Second, and as reflected in the UN Secretary Guidance Note on “The United Nations and Land and Conflict”, land is substantial to any kind of conflict and the improvement of tenure security is key for providing sustainable peace. Land tenure security has proved to be a crucial component for achieving sustainable development. The project’s approach reflects the interdependence of the humanitarian, development and peace initiatives, which cannot be treated separately. Finally, recognizing and addressing the consequences of protracted under-investment in water, sanitation and hygiene facilities that underpin urban inequalities in Iraq is essential for prevention of COVID-19 outbreak. Therefore, to facilitate sustainable and dignified returns of vulnerable displaced persons in Iraq, a comprehensive support addressing multiple needs of the returnees and displaced persons is urgently needed. The proposed program will prioritize vulnerable groups including female heads of household, survivors of violence and trauma, victims of military operations and persons with disability/ies, including older persons.
